title: Nataraja explained
hook: in the temple at Chidambaram, a priest draws back a curtain beside the dancer, and behind it there seems to be nothing at all

segments.voice: Yesterday in Nataraja explained, the flying hair caught the river Ganga, and the dance filled its ring of fire. What did you catch and slow down? Today, the whole dancer, and his home. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-one.
screen: `CATCH WHAT FALLS, AND LET IT GO ON GENTLER.` · `TODAY: THE WHOLE DANCE.`

segments.voice: At Chidambaram, in Tamil Nadu, the dancing Shiva is not in a museum case. He stands in a hall with a golden roof, and he's dressed, garlanded, bathed, and sung to, while a crowd presses forward and oil lamps are waved in the dark. Temple tradition says this is where he danced for two sages who longed to see it: Patanjali, shown with the body of a serpent, and Vyaghrapada, whose name means tiger-foot. And beside the dancer hangs a curtain. At certain moments a priest draws it back, and the people lean in to see what's behind it.
screen: `A HALL WITH A GOLDEN ROOF.` → `THE DANCE FOR TWO SAGES.` → `A CURTAIN BESIDE THE DANCER.`

segments.voice: Behind the curtain there seems to be nothing. An empty space, hung with a garland of golden bilva leaves. It's called the Chidambara rahasya, the secret of Chidambaram. The dancer is there in form, with arms and hair and fire. And right beside him, the same lord, with no form at all. Space. Tradition links this temple with space itself, the open sky the dance happens in. Now put the whole image back together, because a Shaiva teaching does exactly that. It reads the dance as doing five things at once. The drum: creation. The raised hand that says do not fear: preservation, keeping what's made. The flame: dissolution, the ending. The planted foot on Apasmara: concealment, the veil of forgetting that hides what's true. And the lifted foot, the one the elephant hand points to: grace, release. Five acts, one dancer, never stopping. Make, keep, end, hide, free. You've now met each piece across the week: the calm face, the drum, the flame, the pointing hand, the figure underfoot, the hair and the ring. Laid side by side, they make one sentence. Everything moves, and the center is still. One foot lifted, one foot planted. A form you can see, beside a space you can't. And the curtain matters too. The secret isn't locked away. It's shown, on purpose, to anyone standing in the crowd. What's hidden in the image is offered in the same breath as what's seen. The tradition doesn't ask anyone to choose between the dancer and the empty space. It keeps them side by side, behind one curtain.
screen: `THE SECRET: AN EMPTY SPACE.` · `FIVE ACTS: MAKE, KEEP, END, HIDE, FREE.` · `ONE FOOT LIFTED, ONE PLANTED.` · `THE FORM BESIDE THE FORMLESS.` · then, large: `EVERYTHING MOVES, AND THE CENTER IS STILL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: the dance and the space. Settle, and let the breath slow. First, notice everything that's moving: the breath, the heartbeat, sounds coming and going, thoughts flickering at the edges like flames. Let all of it move. Then notice what isn't moving: the space all of it happens in. The room. The quiet behind the sounds. Rest there a few breaths. Then hold both together, the dance and the space, without choosing. If you pray, you can say Shiva's name, or the name of God you use, into that space. The bell holds the time.
Nataraja explained. The whole dancer: five acts in one dance, a calm face in the motion, and beside him at Chidambaram, an empty space that is the same lord without form.
Your line: Nataraja explained. Today, notice one thing that's moving and steady at once: a river, a spinning wheel, a parent rocking a child, your own breath. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-one.

original.note: Sanskrit form of the temple's name, read in tradition as the sky of consciousness; the town is Chidambaram in Tamil Nadu.

trapdoor: what you thought: a famous statue in a temple.
what it means: one dance doing five things at once, worshiped beside an empty space that is the same lord without form.
what a scholar hears: the pancha kritya, the five acts of Shiva in Shaiva Siddhanta, read into the Nataraja image in the Tamil text Unmai Vilakkam.
